title: 2 Kings 4:18–37
context: The son given to the Shunammite later falls ill in the field and dies on his mother’s knees. She lays him on the bed in the prophet’s room, rides urgently to Elisha at Mount Carmel, and clings to his feet in grief. Elisha admits that the LORD has hidden the matter from him. Gehazi goes ahead with Elisha’s staff, but the child does not wake; the mother refuses to leave Elisha, who comes himself, shuts the door, prays to the LORD, and stretches himself on the child until the child sneezes and opens his eyes. The passage is handled as a single unit so that the death, the mother’s lament, and the raising are read together. Both traditions note, as shared ground, the parallel with Elijah and the widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17:17–24) and the later raising of a widow’s son by Jesus (Luke 7:11–17), and both receive the story as a witness to the LORD’s compassion toward the grieving and his power over death.

verses.text: When the child was grown, one day he went out to his father to the reapers.
verses.arminianNotes: The child grows and goes out to his father among the reapers. Arminian readers note the ordinary scene of family life and work, reminding readers that the gift God gave has become part of the everyday rhythm of the household.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the story pauses on this ordinary moment before the sudden trouble, reminding readers that every day is held in God’s hand. Both traditions agree that the narrative lingers on the normal life of the child, which makes the grief that follows all the more poignant.

verses.text: He said to his father, “My head! My head!” He said to his servant, “Carry him to his mother.”
verses.arminianNotes: The boy cries out about his head, and his father sends him to his mother. Arminian readers note the father’s quick response and the tenderness of a family caring for a suffering child, a scene that resonates with every parent’s fear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sudden illness as a reminder that even blessings given by God’s promise remain subject to the frailty of this fallen world. Both traditions agree that the text does not explain the cause of the illness, and that the scene calls for compassion rather than speculation.

verses.text: When he had taken him and brought him to his mother, he sat on her knees until noon, and then died.
verses.arminianNotes: The child sits on his mother’s knees until noon and then dies. Arminian readers respond pastorally to this heartbreaking verse, noting that a mother holding her dying child is among the deepest of sorrows, and that Scripture does not hide such grief from view.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge the depth of this loss and hold that God has not abandoned the family, even though no reason for the death is given. Both traditions agree that the verse invites lament and compassion, and that God’s people may bring such sorrow honestly before him.

verses.text: She went up and laid him on the man of God’s bed, and shut the door on him, and went out.
verses.arminianNotes: She lays him on the man of God’s bed, shuts the door, and goes out. Arminian readers see deliberate faith in her actions, since she places the child where God’s servant rested and does not give him up for burial before seeking help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her actions as an expression of hope that God sustains even in the midst of sorrow. Both traditions agree that she does not yet speak of the death to others, and that her quiet determination points toward the prophet as the one through whom she will seek the LORD’s help.

verses.text: She called to her husband and said, “Please send me one of the servants, and one of the donkeys, that I may run to the man of God and come again.”
verses.arminianNotes: She asks her husband for a servant and a donkey so that she may run to the man of God and return. Arminian readers note her urgency and resolve, showing an active faith that seeks help instead of yielding to despair.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her urgency as the response of faith that God has planted in her heart. Both traditions agree that she acts with focused purpose, turning toward the one through whom God had given her the son, and that her grief moves her to action rather than paralysis.

verses.text: He said, “Why would you want to go to him today? It is not a new moon or a Sabbath.” She said, “It’s all right.”
verses.arminianNotes: Her husband asks why she would go when it is not a new moon or a Sabbath, and she answers that it is all right. Arminian readers note that her reply holds her grief privately until she reaches the man of God, and they see her steadiness as a form of trust under pressure.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the husband’s question may suggest that visits to a prophet were customary on such holy days, and her brief answer shows a faith that does not need to explain itself. Both traditions agree that her composure reflects deep purpose rather than denial, and that the narrative honors her resolve.

verses.text: Then she saddled a donkey, and said to her servant, “Drive, and go forward! Don’t slow down for me, unless I ask you to.”
verses.arminianNotes: She saddles the donkey and tells her servant to drive on without slowing down unless she asks. Arminian readers see her urgency expressed in action, as she presses forward with all her strength to reach the help she seeks.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that her haste reveals both the depth of her need and her confidence that God’s servant can help. Both traditions agree that the verse conveys the intensity of a grieving mother’s determination, and that the narrator invites readers to feel the weight of her journey.

verses.text: So she went, and came to the man of God to Mount Carmel. When the man of God saw her afar off, he said to Gehazi his servant, “Behold, there is the Shunammite.
verses.arminianNotes: She reaches Elisha at Mount Carmel, and he sees her from afar and tells Gehazi that the Shunammite is coming. Arminian readers note Elisha’s attentiveness, recognizing her approach and sensing that her coming at this time is unusual.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers recall that Mount Carmel was the scene of the earlier contest in which the LORD showed himself to be God (1 Kings 18:19–39), and they see the mother traveling to the place associated with God’s servants. Both traditions agree that the verse builds anticipation as she arrives.

verses.text: Please run now to meet her, and ask her, ‘Is it well with you? Is it well with your husband? Is it well with your child?’ ” She answered, “It is well.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gehazi runs to ask whether all is well with her, her husband, and her child, and she answers that it is well. Arminian readers see her answer as a refusal to unburden herself to anyone but the man of God, holding on to hope until she reaches him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in her brief reply a faith that will not surrender to despair before seeking God’s servant. Both traditions agree that her answer is not careless denial but determined reserve, and that her real plea is kept for Elisha himself.

verses.text: When she came to the man of God to the hill, she caught hold of his feet. Gehazi came near to thrust her away; but the man of God said, “Leave her alone, for her soul is troubled within her; and the LORD has hidden it from me, and has not told me.”
verses.arminianNotes: She catches hold of Elisha’s feet, and when Gehazi moves to push her away, Elisha tells him to leave her alone because her soul is troubled and the LORD has hidden the matter from him. Arminian readers note Elisha’s compassion and his honest admission that he does not know everything, which guards against treating prophets as all-knowing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that the LORD reveals or withholds knowledge as he wills, and that even a great prophet depends on God for what he knows. Both traditions agree that Elisha’s gentle response honors the mother’s anguish and models pastoral tenderness toward those in grief.

verses.text: Then she said, “Did I ask you for a son, my lord? Didn’t I say, ‘Do not deceive me’?”
verses.arminianNotes: She asks whether she had asked for a son and reminds Elisha that she had told him not to deceive her. Arminian readers hear the raw honesty of grief in her words, a lament that Scripture allows and that God’s servant must hear with patience and care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a lament that brings pain directly to the one through whom the promise came, and they note that such honest complaint can be part of faith rather than its opposite. Both traditions agree that the mother’s words should be received with compassion, not rebuke.

verses.text: Then he said to Gehazi, “Tuck your cloak into your belt, take my staff in your hand, and go your way. If you meet any man, don’t greet him; and if anyone greets you, don’t answer him again. Then lay my staff on the child’s face.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha sends Gehazi ahead with his staff, telling him not to stop for greetings and to lay the staff on the child’s face. Arminian readers note the urgency of the instructions and the prophet’s desire to act quickly on the grieving mother’s behalf.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the staff, though associated with the prophet, will not by itself bring life, showing that power belongs to the LORD and not to objects. Both traditions agree that the urgency of the command matches the urgency of the mother’s need, and that the story is not over.

verses.text: The child’s mother said, “As the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.” So he arose, and followed her.
verses.arminianNotes: The mother swears by the LORD and by Elisha’s life that she will not leave him, and he rises and follows her. Arminian readers see persevering faith in her refusal to settle for a substitute, and they note that her persistence moves the prophet to come himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her persistence as faith sustained by God, and they note that it echoes Elisha’s own refusal to leave Elijah (2 Kings 2:2, 4, 6). Both traditions agree that her clinging resolve is honored, and that the prophet responds by going personally with her.

verses.text: Gehazi went ahead of them, and laid the staff on the child’s face; but there was no voice and no hearing. Therefore he returned to meet him, and told him, “The child has not awakened.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gehazi lays the staff on the child’s face, but there is no voice and no hearing, and he reports that the child has not awakened. Arminian readers note that the attempt through a substitute fails, highlighting the need for the prophet’s personal presence and prayer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress that no instrument carries power apart from God’s will, and that the failure of the staff points to the LORD as the true source of life. Both traditions agree that the verse heightens the crisis and prepares for the prayer that follows.

verses.text: When Elisha had come into the house, behold, the child was dead, and lying on his bed.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha enters the house and finds the child dead, lying on his bed. Arminian readers note the narrator’s plain acknowledgment of death, which shows the prophet confronting the full reality of the family’s loss without evasion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the narrator’s emphasis that the child was dead as setting the stage for a work only God can do. Both traditions agree that the verse refuses to soften the reality of death, which makes the coming restoration unmistakably the LORD’s act.

verses.text: He went in therefore, and shut the door on them both, and prayed to the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha shuts the door on them both and prays to the LORD. Arminian readers emphasize the role of prayer in this moment, seeing the prophet bring the need before God and trust him to act on behalf of the grieving mother.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that Elisha turns to the LORD, acknowledging that life is in God’s hands alone. Both traditions agree that prayer stands at the center of the miracle, as it did when Elijah prayed for the widow’s son (1 Kings 17:20–21).

verses.text: He went up and lay on the child, and put his mouth on his mouth, and his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. He stretched himself on him; and the child’s flesh grew warm.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha lies on the child, mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, hands to hands, and the child’s flesh grows warm. Arminian readers note the physical and personal engagement of the prophet, who identifies himself fully with the child as he seeks God’s restoring power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the returning warmth as the beginning of God’s restoring work, accomplished through his servant but not by his servant’s power. Both traditions agree that the act parallels Elijah stretching himself on the widow’s son (1 Kings 17:21), and that the text does not present it as a technique.

verses.text: Then he returned, and walked in the house once back and forth, then went up and stretched himself out on him. Then the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha walks back and forth in the house, stretches himself on the child again, and the child sneezes seven times and opens his eyes. Arminian readers note the prophet’s perseverance in prayer and action, and they see the gradual restoration as an encouragement to persist in seeking God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the child’s opening eyes the LORD’s power over death, completing the work he began. Both traditions agree that the restoration of life is a gift of God and a sign of his compassion toward the grieving mother, who had refused to let go of hope.

verses.text: He called Gehazi, and said, “Call this Shunammite!” So he called her. When she had come in to him, he said, “Take up your son.”
verses.arminianNotes: Elisha has Gehazi call the Shunammite and tells her to take up her son. Arminian readers note the tenderness of the moment, as the son is returned to the mother who would not give up her hope or her plea.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s faithfulness in giving back the son he first promised. Both traditions agree that the scene parallels Elijah returning the widow’s son to her (1 Kings 17:23) and Jesus giving a raised son back to his mother (Luke 7:15), as shared witness to God’s compassion.

verses.text: Then she went in, fell at his feet, and bowed herself to the ground; then she picked up her son, and went out.
verses.arminianNotes: She falls at Elisha’s feet, bows herself to the ground, takes up her son, and goes out. Arminian readers see her worshipful gratitude as the fitting response to God’s mercy, completing a story of faith that was tested and honored.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her humble bowing as an acknowledgment that this restoration came from the LORD through his servant. Both traditions agree that the story ends in wordless gratitude, and that Hebrews 11:35 later remembers women who received their dead raised to life as part of the witness of faith.
